bib.title: Transformers as Soft Reasoners over Language

question: Can transformers be trained to reason (or emulate reasoning) over facts and rules stated in natural-language sentences, including at depths unseen in training?
hypothesis: Transformers can act as limited soft theorem provers over explicit theories expressed in language.
contributions: Transformers learn to reason with rules (99% accuracy, generalising to deeper depths)
Zero-shot transfer to two hand-authored rulebases
Transfer to crowdsourced paraphrased rules (98% when trained)
Model identifies facts an answer depends on (94% F1 claimed in intro)
BERT and ESIM also learn the tasks, with lower scores

method.summary: Synthetic rulebases (facts + conjunctive rules, closed-world, negation as failure) are generated in logic, forward-chained to label True/False questions, rendered in templated English, and used to fine-tune RoBERTa-large (pre-fine-tuned on RACE) as a binary classifier. Evaluated on held-out depths, perturbed theories, two hand-written rulebases, and crowdsourced paraphrases.

datasets.name: D=0, D<=1, D<=2, D<=3, DMax (synthetic rulebases)
datasets.size: 100k examples each (25k per Type x with/without negation); theories have 1-16 facts and 1-9 rules
datasets.split: 70/10/20 train/dev/test, no theory overlap between partitions
datasets.preprocessing: Templates: 'If condition [and condition]* then conclusion.', 'All attribute* people|things are attribute.', 'attribute* people|things are attribute.'; DMax goes to depth 5

datasets.name: Birds (Birds1, Birds2)
datasets.source: Sergot's formulation of the birds puzzle (McCarthy 1984)

datasets.name: ParaRules
datasets.size: 40k questions over about 2k theories (from 10k generated theories)
datasets.source: crowdworker paraphrases of Type 1 no-negation theories
datasets.preprocessing: rephrasings auto-checked for key attributes; at least depth 3 required

other.input: [CLS] context [SEP] statement [SEP]; [CLS] projected to a single logit, >0 = true

other.hyperparameters: fixed, inherited from RoBERTa on RACE (Liu et al. 2019); values not printed

inference.samples: single evaluation per model; no seeds or runs stated

metrics.name: accuracy
metrics.definition: fraction of true/false questions answered correctly; test sets balanced so random is 50%

metrics.name: critical-sentence P/R/F1
metrics.definition: per question, sentences whose removal flips a true prediction to false vs. sentences in all proofs; macro-averaged

eval.protocol: Train on D=0,<=1,<=2,<=3,Max; test on DMax test sliced by depth; sentence-removal perturbation on no-negation half of DMax test; zero-shot on Birds/Electricity/ParaRules.

results.claim: Trained RoBERTa masters the held-out test of its own dataset.
results.setup: RoBERTa-large, trained and tested on DMax-style synthetic data
results.quote: RoBERTa is able to master the test data almost perfectly (99% accuracy, row 1)

results.claim: A model trained to depth 3 generalises to depth 5 problems.
results.setup: D<=3 model tested on Depth=5 slice of DMax
results.quote: the D≤3 model generalizes well right up to the maximum depth tested (e..g, 97.6% for Depth=5 problems)

results.claim: A model trained to depth 2 reaches 71.1% on unseen depth 3.
results.setup: D<=2 model on Depth=3 slice of DMax

results.claim: Removing a critical sentence flips a true prediction to false only 81% of the time (a formal prover would do 100%).
results.setup: DMax no-negation test; 113978 sentence-removed probes, 20746 with critical sentence removed
results.quote: we observe this happens 81% of the time (16654/(16654+3895))

results.claim: Accuracy on theories with a critical sentence removed falls to 81.2% versus 99.4% on originals.
results.note: Table 2 columns: Original 99.4, Remove Irrelevant 99.6, Remove Critical 81.2, Remove Any 96.3 (column order inferred from layout)

results.claim: Zero-shot, the strongest model MMax scores 66.6% on crowdsourced-paraphrase rules.
results.quote: partially solves this dataset with a score of 66.6%

results.claim: Training on D<=3 plus ParaRules gives 98.8% on ParaRules test.
results.setup: RoBERTa trained on D<=3 and ParaRules train partitions
results.quote: has an accuracy of 98.8% on ParaRules test

results.claim: Predicting critical sentences reaches macro F1 of 92.4.
Replacing every word with a random word drops accuracy to 83.3% from 99.3%, so pretrained knowledge matters.
results.quote: RoBERTa scores 83.3% on the test partition, substantially below the original 99.3%

results.claim: Zero-shot failure on Electricity4: higher-depth models do slightly worse than the depth-1 model, a blind spot from rare training patterns.
results.setup: models trained at deeper depths, Electricity4
results.quote: the trained model can have unanticipated blind spots

results.claim: Mod0 scores below random at depths above 2 because it predicts false for everything not given.
results.quote: Mod0 scores worse than random (50%) at depths higher than 2

limits: Small theories (<20 facts, <10 rules), small domains (<100 ground facts), at most one universally quantified variable per rule.
Synthetic templated language; paraphrase test is only a first step, not arbitrary natural language.
Authors leave open whether the transformer is actually reasoning; it emulates i/o behaviour.
Closed-world/negation-as-failure semantics clash with NLI intuition.
Perturbation analysis excludes negation because of non-monotonicity.
Training hyperparameters, compute and seeds not stated; Tables 1, 4, 5, 6 numbers are not in the extracted text, so only prose-quoted numbers are recorded.
Predates LLM-era few-shot prompting; models are fine-tuned RoBERTa, not prompted.
